body:
There's two issues with this:

1. We still lack a good definition of how `multipart/form-data` works in practice: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/6424.
2. We cannot start sending requests that are rather different from how forms have always worked across the origin boundary without some kind of server-side opt-in, such as a CORS preflight. (Some people are pushing a solution for this for more HTTP methods, but I don't think it has been thoroughly vetted just yet.)

The web platform includes a multipart/form-data parser API, in the `formData` method of fetch requests and responses; and while the specification for that is incomplete, it says that the presence of a filename in the `Content-Disposition` header is what determines whether an entry is a file – and if there isn't one, the `Content-Type` is dropped. For some server-side JavaScript runtimes such as Deno, Bun and Cloudflare Workers, *this is the most common way to parse multipart/form-data requests.*

From what I can tell, this pattern (treating an entry as a file if and only if it has a filename, and dropping the `Content-Type` otherwise) seems to also hold for many other server-side languages and libraries. So we can assume that the vast majority of servers won't be able to properly parse such request bodies, and as @annevk says, we'd need a way to know that a particular server can deal with this input before sending it.

> The web platform includes a multipart/form-data parser API, in the `formData` method of fetch requests and responses; and while the specification for that is incomplete

As a side note, I think not enough people are aware of your excellent work in https://andreubotella.github.io/multipart-form-data/ . For jsdom, [I had to reimplement a multipart/form-data parser](https://github.com/jsdom/jsdom/pull/3850), and was very dismayed when reading the RFC at how useless it was for that purpose. I thankfully found the spec you wrote, and was able to follow it line-by-line to get a great result.

I've examined some other server frameworks, and as far I can tell

- Spring
  - Won't break when `Content-Type` is present on non-file part, but usually part headers aren't accessible
  - `Content-Type` header is accessible via [Part#headers()](https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/current/javadoc-api/org/springframework/http/codec/multipart/Part.html#headers()) when receiving as `@RequestPart Flux<Part> aPart`, as any other header
- http4s / http4k / Ktor
  - `Content-Type` is accessible via `headers` or `contentType` methods/properties on any parts
  - Discrimination between 'file' or 'non-file' is based on `; filename="…"` presence
- Django
  - `MultiPartParser` exists, however it has to be set manually as parser, and one can provide a different (self-written or third-party) parser
    - File / non-file decision is based on `; filename="…"`
    - All headers are parsed by `Parser` in `http/multipartparser.py`, but not all of them are handled by `MultiPartParser`
    - `MultiPartParser` handles `Content-Disposition` (of course) and `Content-Transfer-Encoding` (when set to `base64`) for all parts, plus `Content-Length` and `Content-Type` for files, dropping any other headers
- Servant
  - Only `Content-Type` header on files supported, other headers aren't accessible via `Servant.Multipart` API
- PHP (default parser / request_parse_body)
  - No support for headers at all, all 'files' are _saved_ and can be found via `$_FILES`, other fields are just strings in `$_POST`; even uploading many files with the same `name` in disposition is tricky

So, there are server frameworks which can use `Content-Type` value without `; filename`, and there are others which cannot even access individual part headers at all. Behavior of latter _almost_ conforms to the Section 4.8 with one exception: `Content-Type` header is explicitly permitted, but ignored.

Therefore, I argue that multipart parsers — including browsers — should not treat parts with a `Content-Type` but no `filename` as "files". Instead, such parts should be treated as structured content and mapped based on their `Content-Type`, defaulting to `text/plain` when omitted.

While current browser behavior only sets `Content-Type` on `Blobs` or `Files` (and always includes filename), this design discourages semantic use of MIME types for non-file parts. Allowing a way to set `Content-Type` without triggering filename would align with many server frameworks, which already support this pattern.
